note.explanation: A balanced chemical equation gives the mole ratio between reactants and products. Use that ratio to work out the amount of a substance that reacts or forms, then convert between moles and mass or particles if needed.
examples: In CaCO₃ + 2HCl → CaCl₂ + H₂O + CO₂, 100 g of CaCO₃ produces 111 g of CaCl₂.
In 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O, 4 g of H₂ produces 36 g of H₂O.
note.simple: The numbers in a balanced equation act like a recipe. They show how much of each substance reacts and how much product is made.
note.checkQuestion: How much CO₂ is produced when 10 g of CH₄ reacts with excess oxygen according to CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O?
note.title: Calculations from a chemical equation
steps: Use its coefficients to find the mole ratio, or use the molar masses to find the mass ratio.
Set up the ratio for the amount given in the question.
Calculate the required mass, moles, or number of particles.
note.answer: A balanced chemical equation gives the mole ratio between reactants and products. This ratio can be used to calculate how much of a substance reacts or is produced.

mcqs.stem: According to 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O, how many moles of O₂ react with 6 moles of H₂?
rationales: This is incorrect because the equation requires 1 mole of O₂ for every 2 moles of H₂.
This is correct because the ratio is 2:1, so 6 moles of H₂ require 3 moles of O₂.
This is incorrect because 4 moles of O₂ would require 8 moles of H₂.
This is incorrect because 6 moles of O₂ would require 12 moles of H₂.

mcqs.stem: What mass of CO₂ is produced by the complete reaction of 16 g of CH₄ with excess oxygen? CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O
rationales: This is incorrect because 11 g is one quarter of the required product mass.
This is incorrect because it is half of the mass produced by 16 g of CH₄.
This is correct because 16 g of CH₄ is 1 mole and the equation produces 1 mole, or 44 g, of CO₂.
This is incorrect because it is twice the mass produced by 16 g of CH₄.

mcqs.stem: According to 4Al + 3O₂ → 2Al₂O₃, what mass of oxygen reacts with 0.3 moles of aluminium?
rationales: This is incorrect because it does not use the 3:4 mole ratio of O₂ to Al correctly.
This is correct: 0.3 × 3/4 = 0.225 mol O₂, and 0.225 × 32 = 7.2 g.
This is incorrect because it is twice the correct mass.
This is incorrect because it is three times the correct mass.

mcqs.stem: What mass of water forms when 5 g of hydrogen reacts with excess oxygen? 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O
rationales: This is incorrect because 18 g is the mass of only 1 mole of water.
This is incorrect because 36 g of water forms from 4 g of hydrogen, not 5 g.
This is correct because 4 g of hydrogen produces 36 g of water, so 5 g produces 36/4 × 5 = 45 g.
This is incorrect because it is more than the mass produced by the stated ratio.

mcqs.stem: How many moles of CO₂ form when 2.25 moles of ethanol burn completely? C₂H₅OH + 3O₂ → 2CO₂ + 3H₂O
rationales: This is incorrect because it is less than the amount given by the 2:1 ratio.
This is incorrect because it does not apply the coefficient ratio of 2 moles of CO₂ per mole of ethanol.
This is correct because 2.25 × 2 = 4.5 moles of CO₂.
This is incorrect because it is greater than the amount given by the equation.

mcqs.stem: What mass of CaCl₂ forms from 25 g of CaCO₃, if hydrochloric acid is in excess? CaCO₃ + 2HCl → CaCl₂ + H₂O + CO₂
rationales: This is correct because 100 g of CaCO₃ produces 111 g of CaCl₂, so 25 g produces 111/100 × 25 = 27.75 g.
This is incorrect because it repeats the starting mass rather than using the mass ratio.
This is incorrect because 111 g of CaCl₂ forms from 100 g of CaCO₃.
This is incorrect because it is one tenth of the correctly calculated product mass.

written.text: 25g of limestone (CaCO₃) reacts with an excess of hydrochloric acid according to the above equation. How much calcium chloride (CaCl₂) will be produced?

rubric.why: The correct mass relationship must be taken from the equation.
rubric.description: Uses the equation's mass ratio for CaCO₃ and CaCl₂.
rubric.how: State that 100 g of CaCO₃ produces 111 g of CaCl₂.

rubric.why: The final product mass is the quantity asked for.
rubric.description: Calculates and states the mass of CaCl₂.
rubric.how: Apply 111/100 × 25 and give the answer with units.

modelAnswer: Mass of CaCO₃ = 25 g
Molar mass of CaCO₃ = 100 g mol⁻¹
Mass of CaCl₂ product = ?
Molar mass of CaCl₂ = 111 g mol⁻¹
According to the equation
100 g of limestone reacts to produce calcium chloride = 111 g
1 g of limestone will react to produce calcium chloride = 111/100 g
25 g of limestone will react to produce calcium chloride = 111/100 × 25

written.text: 1.80 moles of ethyl alcohol, when burnt in air completely, will utilize how many moles of oxygen gas? Also calculate the number of moles of CO₂ produced.
written.finalAnswer: 5.4 moles of O₂ and 3.6 moles of CO₂

rubric.why: The equation coefficients establish the required mole ratios.
rubric.description: Writes the balanced equation.

rubric.why: The oxygen amount must follow the coefficient ratio.
rubric.description: Calculates moles of oxygen.

rubric.why: The carbon dioxide amount must follow its coefficient in the equation.
rubric.description: Calculates moles of carbon dioxide.

rubric.why: Both requested quantities must be stated clearly.
rubric.description: States the final amounts with substance names and units.
rubric.how: Give 5.4 moles of O₂ and 3.6 moles of CO₂.

modelAnswer: No. of moles of ethyl alcohol = 1.80
No. of moles of oxygen needed = ?
C₂H₅OH (l) + 3O₂ (g) → 2CO₂ (g) + 3H₂O (g)
One mole of ethyl alcohol, when completely burnt, needs oxygen = 3 moles
1.8 moles of ethyl alcohol, upon burning, will need oxygen = 3/1 × 1.8
= 5.4 moles
1 mole of ethyl alcohol produces moles of CO₂ = 2.0
1.8 mol of ethyl alcohol will produce = 2/1 × 1.8
= 3.6 moles

written.text: Aluminium metal reacts with oxygen to produce aluminium oxide. How many grams of oxygen will be required to react completely with 0.3 moles of aluminium?

rubric.why: The balanced equation gives the mole ratio needed for the calculation.
rubric.description: Writes the balanced chemical equation.

rubric.why: The calculation must convert the given aluminium moles to oxygen moles.
rubric.description: Finds the moles of oxygen.

rubric.why: Oxygen moles must be converted to mass using its molar mass.
rubric.description: Uses the molar mass of O₂ to calculate the mass.

rubric.why: The final oxygen mass is the requested result.
rubric.description: States the final mass of oxygen.

modelAnswer: Moles of Al = 0.3
Grams of O₂ used = ?
4Al (s) + 3O₂ (g) → 2Al₂O₃ (s)
4 moles of aluminium need oxygen = 3.0 moles
1.0 mole of aluminium will need oxygen = 3/4
0.3 moles of aluminium will need oxygen = 3/4 × 0.3
= 0.225 moles
1 mole of oxygen (O₂) has molar mass = 32 g
0.225 mole of oxygen (O₂) will have molar mass = 32 × 0.225

written.text: How many molecules of water will be produced if we react 5 g of hydrogen gas with excess of oxygen gas?

rubric.why: The balanced equation establishes the reactant and product relationship.
rubric.description: Writes the balanced equation and its mass relationship.
rubric.how: Use 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O and identify 4 g H₂ producing 36 g H₂O.

rubric.why: The water mass is needed before its molecules can be found.
rubric.description: Calculates the mass of water produced.

rubric.why: The molecules in 36 g of water provide the next conversion ratio.
rubric.description: Finds the molecules in 36 g of water.

rubric.why: The amount of water must be scaled from 36 g to 45 g.
rubric.description: Scales the molecule count to 45 g.

rubric.why: The final answer must be the number of water molecules.
rubric.description: States the final number of molecules.

modelAnswer: Mass of H₂ used = 5g
Molecules of water produced = ?
2H₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2H₂O(l)
2 moles  1 mole  2 moles
4 g of hydrogen produce H₂O = 36 g of H₂O
5 g of hydrogen will produce H₂O = 36/4 × 5 = 45g of H₂O
18g (1 mole) of H₂O contain molecules = 6.022 × 10²³
36g of H₂O contain molecules = 6.022 × 10²³ × 2
45g of H₂O contain = 45/36 × 12.04 × 10²³
= 1.505 × 10²⁴ molecules

written.finalAnswer: Balance the chemical equation, use its mole ratio and the molar masses, then calculate the product masses.

written.text:
How many grams of CO₂ will be produced when we react 10 g of CH₄ with excess of O₂ according to the following equation?

CH₄(g) + 2O₂(g) → CO₂(g) + 2H₂O(g)

rubric.why: The reactant-to-product mass ratio is essential to the calculation.
rubric.description: Identifies the masses corresponding to the equation.
rubric.how: Use 16 g CH₄ to produce 44 g CO₂.

rubric.why: The given reactant mass must be scaled by the correct mass ratio.
rubric.description: Sets up the mass-ratio calculation.

rubric.why: The calculation must give the amount of CO₂ formed.
rubric.description: Calculates the carbon dioxide mass.

rubric.why: The final answer must include the correct product and unit.
rubric.description: States the final mass of CO₂.

modelAnswer: CH₄(g) + 2O₂(g) → CO₂(g) + 2H₂O(g)
Molar mass of CH₄ = 16 g mol⁻¹
Molar mass of CO₂ = 44 g mol⁻¹
16 g of CH₄ will produce CO₂ = 44 g
10 g of CH₄ will produce CO₂ = 44/16 × 10

written.text:
How many moles of coal are needed to produce 10 moles of CO according to the following equation?

3C(s) + O₂(g) + H₂O(l) → H₂(g) + 3CO(g)

rubric.why: The equation supplies the ratio between carbon in coal and CO.
rubric.description: Uses the given equation's coefficients.
rubric.how: Identify the 3:3 ratio of C to CO.

rubric.why: The mole ratio determines the amount of coal needed.
rubric.description: Finds the carbon-to-CO mole ratio.
rubric.how: Show that the ratio simplifies to 1:1.

rubric.why: The ratio must be applied to the 10 moles of CO.
rubric.description: Calculates the amount of carbon needed.

rubric.why: The final amount and unit must answer the question.
rubric.description: States the required amount of coal.

modelAnswer: 3C(s) + O₂(g) + H₂O(l) → H₂(g) + 3CO(g)
3 moles of C produce 3 moles of CO
Moles of coal (C) needed for 10 moles of CO = 3/3 × 10
= 10 moles

written.text:
How much SO₂ is needed in grams to produce 10 moles of sulphur?

2H₂S(g) + SO₂(g) → 2H₂O(l) + 3S(s)

rubric.why: The balanced equation gives the mole ratio of SO₂ to sulphur.
rubric.description: Uses the equation's coefficient ratio.
rubric.how: Identify that 1 mole of SO₂ produces 3 moles of S.

rubric.why: The required SO₂ moles must be found from the sulphur amount.
rubric.description: Calculates moles of SO₂.

rubric.why: The molar mass is needed to convert SO₂ moles to grams.
rubric.description: Finds the molar mass of SO₂.

rubric.why: The mass must be calculated from the correct mole amount and molar mass.
rubric.description: Multiplies SO₂ moles by its molar mass.

rubric.why: The final answer must be the required SO₂ mass.
rubric.description: States the final mass with units.

modelAnswer: 2H₂S(g) + SO₂(g) → 2H₂O(l) + 3S(s)
1 mole of SO₂ produces 3 moles of S
Moles of SO₂ needed to produce 10 moles of S = 10/3
Molar mass of SO₂ = 32 + 2(16) = 64 g mol⁻¹
Mass of SO₂ = 10/3 × 64

written.text:
How much ammonia is needed in grams to produce 1 kg of urea fertilizer?

2NH₃(aq) + CO₂(aq) → CO(NH₂)₂(aq) + H₂O(l)

rubric.why: The balanced equation gives the ratio between ammonia and urea.
rubric.description: Uses the equation's mole relationship.
rubric.how: Identify that 2 moles of NH₃ produce 1 mole of urea.

rubric.why: The ammonia mass corresponding to the equation is needed.
rubric.description: Finds the mass of 2 moles of NH₃.

rubric.why: The urea molar mass links its amount to its mass.
rubric.description: Finds the molar mass of urea.

rubric.why: The mass ratio must be applied to 1 kg of urea.
rubric.description: Sets up the mass-ratio calculation.

rubric.why: The answer must give the required ammonia mass.
rubric.description: States the final mass of ammonia.

modelAnswer: 2NH₃(aq) + CO₂(aq) → CO(NH₂)₂(aq) + H₂O(l)
2 moles of NH₃ produce 1 mole of urea
Molar mass of NH₃ = 17 g mol⁻¹
Mass of 2 moles of NH₃ = 2 × 17 = 34 g
Molar mass of urea, CO(NH₂)₂ = 12 + 16 + 2(14) + 4(1) = 60 g mol⁻¹
60 g of urea require NH₃ = 34 g
1000 g of urea require NH₃ = 34/60 × 1000

examTips: Numerical questions may ask you to find a reactant or product mass, moles, or number of particles from a balanced equation.
Write the balanced equation first and show the coefficients clearly; they provide the mole ratio.
For mass calculations, show the molar masses or the mass ratio before substituting the given amount.
For a multi-step question, show each conversion, such as grams to moles or moles to particles, and include the unit in the final answer.

explain.title: A balanced equation is a recipe
explain.body: A balanced chemical equation tells you the relative numbers of moles that react and form. The coefficients are the mole ratio.

explain.title: Use the ratio for masses
explain.body: Find the molar mass of each substance. Combine these masses with the mole ratio to get the mass ratio, then scale it to the amount given in the question.

explain.title: Convert to the quantity asked for
explain.body: Some questions ask for moles or particles rather than grams. Use the equation ratio first, then use molar mass or Avogadro's number for any further conversion.

explain.title: Keep the equation correct
explain.body: A chemical equation tells the reacting and producing elements or compounds in a chemical reaction. It also tells the mole ratio between reactants or products and between reactants and products. A chemical equation must be balanced and should show the correct formulas of all the participating elements and compounds.

explain.title: Mass ratios come from mole ratios
explain.body: The mole ratio between reactants and products as shown by a chemical equation enables us to find out the mass ratio of these substances. A chemical equation is used to calculate the masses of the reactants as well as the products, which take part in a chemical reaction.

mistakes: Using an unbalanced equation or incorrect chemical formula gives the wrong mole ratio.
Using the coefficients as a mass ratio without taking molar masses into account.
Reversing the ratio—for example, using reactant mass divided by product mass when the opposite is needed.
Leaving out a conversion step when changing grams to moles or moles to particles.
Giving a number without naming the substance or including its unit.
